rows: Specified food and feed products require authorisation before sale in the UK.
Regulated categories include novel foods, additives, flavourings and other defined products.
Applicants should provide evidence relevant to safety and proposed use.
Authorisation can include conditions, specifications and restrictions.
Official registers record authorisation status for Great Britain.
Businesses should ensure the exact product and intended use are authorised.
Material changes to identity, process or use may require reassessment.
Submission of an application or similarity to an authorised product does not permit market placement.
Conclusions require exact identity, process, intended use, application status, decision and register evidence.
Food businesses must manage chemical hazards that could make food unsafe.
Chemical contaminants can arise from environment, agriculture, processing or packaging.
Relevant contaminants include mycotoxins, process contaminants and persistent pollutants.
Businesses should identify foreseeable contaminants in their hazard analysis.
Supplier controls and specifications can reduce chemical risk.
Legal limits or action levels apply to some contaminants.
Sampling and laboratory testing may be needed to verify control.
Non-compliant results should trigger investigation, product action and corrective measures.
A supplier certificate or single compliant sample does not prove every batch is safe.
Conclusions require contaminant, product, source, limit, sampling, laboratory, distribution and corrective-action evidence.
Natural mineral water, spring water and bottled drinking water are distinct regulated categories.
Natural mineral water requires formal recognition before marketing under that description.
Source protection and hygienic abstraction are fundamental controls.
Treatment options differ between water categories.
Bottling should protect the water from contamination.
Labels must use the correct category and required information.
Composition, microbiological and chemical requirements must be met.
Changes to source, treatment or product should be assessed for regulatory impact.
A spring name or clear appearance does not establish compliance with bottled-water rules.
Conclusions require source, recognition, abstraction, treatment, analysis, bottling, label and traceability evidence.
Nutrition and health claims in commercial communications must comply with specific rules.
The Great Britain register lists authorised and non-authorised claims.
A nutrition claim must meet the applicable conditions of use.
A health claim must use authorised wording or have the same consumer meaning where permitted.
Claims must not be false, ambiguous or misleading.
Food cannot be claimed to treat, prevent or cure disease.
Relevant mandatory information should accompany claims where required.
Businesses should check the current register before launching or changing a claim.
A scientifically plausible statement or competitor claim does not prove that a claim is authorised.
Conclusions require exact wording, product composition, conditions, audience, context, register and label evidence.
